title: Notes in translation
bodyMd:
A translator working on a fictional nineteenth-century diary faced an unfamiliar local expression. A literal translation sounded odd, while a smooth modern equivalent removed a distinction important to the writer’s account of village life. She chose a slightly unfamiliar phrase and added a short note.

An editor worried that notes would interrupt the reader. The translator agreed that too many could turn the diary into a reference manual, but argued that removing every difficulty would create a misleading impression of effortless familiarity. She used notes only where a misunderstanding would alter the reader’s interpretation, not for every unusual word. Her aim was neither to reproduce every obstacle of the original nor to erase its distance from the present. The translation was a guided encounter with another setting, requiring decisions about which differences mattered.
